prompt.context: The client is an engine manufacturer that designs and builds engines for large commercial trucks. They have designed a new engine with significant new technology and significant new content. It will meet all federal guidelines for at least 10 years. The client has spent significant R&D money on this engine and expects to be able to charge a premium price to recoup the investment. However, the client's largest customer, representing 60% of all sales, has been complaining about quality. Research has shown that although the client promised customers soot emissions less than 3k ppm, they are currently seeing 20k ppm (ppm = parts per million).
prompt.question: What is wrong and what should they do?

clarifying_info.q: What changed in the product design for this new engine?
clarifying_info.a: The design process was unchanged. All testing was done the same as with historical products. However, the FMEA analysis (Failure Modes and Effects Analysis) was skimped on. The significant new technological components were developed according to the client's standard process.

clarifying_info.q: Is there an issue with the manufacturing workforce or assembly process?
clarifying_info.a: The plant uses a highly skilled and educated workforce. There is no learning curve associated with the assembly of this product.

clarifying_info.q: How does the client handle field service and warranty reporting?
clarifying_info.a: The client utilizes field technicians at the customer site. They are the ones reporting the warranty data to the client. They are well educated on the product.

clarifying_info.q: Has anything changed in how parts and sub-assemblies are sourced?
clarifying_info.a: Traditionally the client used few suppliers who delivered large sub-assemblies. Now, in an effort to save costs, they have sourced many more suppliers to get the best price for each component and are choosing to do more of the assembly themselves. However, all of these suppliers are delivering products that meet the specifications delivered by engineering.

clarifying_info.q: What are the top warranty issues being reported?
clarifying_info.a: A Pareto chart of top warranty issues is available — the majority of warranty claims relate to leaks and lost/missing parts.

framework: Understand what changed in the product design vs. the last model and whether the new design meets customer requirements
Examine the manufacturing process: technology used, labor, process changes that may not have been implemented
Investigate the parts supply chain: changes in supplier base, component specifications, and sub-assembly procurement
Review defect/warranty data: identify the main symptoms customers are reporting and compare with the previous engine

questions.prompt: Based on the information provided about design, manufacturing, service, and procurement, where does the root cause of the quality problem lie?
questions.guidance: The candidate should work through each area and eliminate red herrings. Design process was unchanged; workforce is skilled with no learning curve; field technicians are well-educated. The key change is in procurement: the client shifted from few suppliers delivering large sub-assemblies to many suppliers delivering individual components. Although each supplier meets its specification, specifications for individual components were written with tolerances appropriate for sub-assemblies. The stack-up of tolerances across many individually-acceptable components causes poor fit, resulting in leaks and lost parts — which explains the soot emissions spike from <3k ppm to 20k ppm. The FMEA being skimped on is a contributing factor (the tolerance stack-up risk was not identified).

questions.prompt: What recommendations would you make to the client to resolve the problem?
questions.guidance: Strong answers present multiple options with trade-offs. Three main options: (1) Tighten tolerances on individually procured parts — more expensive to enforce but addresses root cause directly; candidate should note a cost-benefit analysis is needed. (2) Increase end-product testing / quality inspection before shipment — increases manufacturing time and cost but reduces warranty claims reaching the field. (3) Revert to ordering sub-assemblies from fewer integrated suppliers — more expensive per unit but eliminates tolerance stack-up; candidate should compare cost of this option vs. option 1. Risks to call out: tightening tolerances may require suppliers to invest in better equipment (cost pass-through); increased testing adds cycle time; reverting to sub-assemblies may not be feasible if supplier relationships have changed.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the risks associated with each recommended course of action?

categories.name: Tighten component tolerances
ideas: Suppliers may need capital investment to achieve tighter tolerances, leading to price increases
Some suppliers may be unable to meet tighter specs and exit, reducing supply base
Longer qualification and validation time before issue is resolved
May require re-negotiation of all supplier contracts

categories.name: Increase end-product testing
ideas: Adds time to manufacturing cycle, potentially delaying deliveries
Does not fix root cause — defective assemblies still produced, just caught later
Testing may not catch all failure modes (field conditions differ from test bench)

categories.name: Revert to sub-assembly procurement
ideas: Higher unit cost for sub-assemblies vs. individual components
Requires re-establishing or renegotiating relationships with sub-assembly suppliers
May reduce client's internal assembly capability and control over the process
Transition period where both models coexist creates complexity

recommendation: The root cause is tolerance stack-up resulting from the shift to individual-component procurement from many suppliers — each component meets spec individually, but their combined tolerances cause poor fit, leaks, and lost parts driving emissions from <3k ppm to 20k ppm
Recommended immediate action: increase end-product testing to stem warranty claims while a longer-term fix is implemented
Recommended long-term action: tighten tolerances on procured components or revert to sub-assembly procurement — conduct a cost-benefit analysis to choose between these two options
Additionally, reinstate rigorous FMEA analysis for new product introductions to catch tolerance stack-up and similar integration risks early
risks: Tightening tolerances increases supplier costs and may not be achievable by all current suppliers
Reverting to sub-assembly procurement increases unit cost and requires supplier re-engagement
Increased testing extends manufacturing lead time and adds cost without eliminating the root cause
Delay in resolution risks losing the client's largest customer (60% of sales)
next_steps: Quantify the cost of each option (tolerance tightening vs. sub-assembly reversion vs. increased testing) via a cost-benefit analysis
Assess supplier capability to meet tighter tolerances before committing to that path
Implement interim end-product testing immediately to reduce warranty exposure
Commission a full FMEA review for the new engine to identify any other unaddressed risk areas
